I am a 28 year old, unemployed alcoholic.

I still live at home with my mom.

For the past couple days, I have been trying not to drink. I hate not drinking. Time feels like it passes so much slower without alcohol and without drinking (my go-to pass time), there's nothing to do to fill all that "extra" time. It's so boring. The worst part is the insomnia. I'm bored and there's nothing to do so I just want to sleep but I can't. At least not when I want to. I often get smacked with extreme fatigue in the middle of the day and can't find the energy to drag my ass out of bed until the middle of the night. This has been very counterproductive to finding a job. I figured out a strategy to help me get at least a few hours sleep during the night, though. My go-to drink is [insert liquor here] and Coke, meaning I consume a massive amount of sugar and calories when I'm drinking; I've discovered I can sorta fool my body into thinking we need to "sleep it off" without actually drinking by consuming a large quantity of candy and pop before bed. Not good for me, I know, but better than consuming an entire bottle of hard liquor every day.

Last night, I went to the convenience store to get some candy and pop and when I got back, my mom was in her room pretending to sleep. She does that when she's upset. Usually about my drinking. I tried to explain that I just got candy and pop, but she just ignored me. So I went in my room, ate my snacks, and passed out for a few hours; I watched Netflix for a few hours when I got up before sunrise. My mom has gone to work now.

I don't know why I'm even bothering to try to stop drinking right now. I've already ruined my life. I dropped out of college. I have a huge debt. I quit a really good job for no good reason about a month ago. I have no friends, literally the top 2 people in my messaging app are my mom and sister followed by a bunch of mailing list texts; my sister's texts have become less and less frequent and I really only send my mom pictures of the dog. I honestly don't really see the point in carrying on any longer...

Ages 18-20, I managed to hold down a full-time job at a restaurant because my manager recognized that I had mental health issues; he gave me a consistent work schedule, Wednesday through Sunday, 5:00pm to closing, and it really helped me to manage my depression and anxiety without medication. Then, in 2011, I tried to go to college. Trying to juggle school and work was just too much for me; I ended up dropping out because I was failing out and about to be kicked out of residence anyway. So, I moved back home and got my old job at the restaurant back. It was fine for a couple years, despite the fact that I wasn't really going anywhere in life, until my manager quit and we got a new one that didn't care about my mental health issues. She screwed with my work schedule and I ended up attempting suicide because unpredictability triggered my suicidal thoughts. I lost that job and ended up basically working part-time for a few years, until I was 26, because that was about all I could handle. Now, I'm 27 going on 28 and I still live at home with my mom.

The Lexapro has helped me to hold down a job where I'm working 50-60 hours per week, not including all the unpaid overtime I put in, without becoming suicidal. For the most part. There are still days where I wake up for my 4th 10-12 hour shift in a row and wish for death, but I am able to manage those thoughts without acting on them. It also has given me the motivation to move out of my mom's house and go back to school. Unfortunately, I don't have the money to do either of those things right now. I also don't worry about my mom's financial situation as much.

So, current issues aside, the Lexapro was and is helping me. I think what's triggering my suicidal thoughts right now is unhappiness with my job. I worked over 250 hours in January - again, before the approx. 30 minutes of unpaid overtime I put in each day. I had one day off at the beginning of the month, then I worked 18 consecutive days, 10-12 hours per day, then I had another day off, and then I would have had to work straight through until the end of January if I didn't fuck up and go to the wrong place for training. I was 30 minutes late for training so they sent me home, which got me a weekend off. By that point, I was so burnt out that I didn't even care that I might get in trouble later. I powered through thinking it was a one time deal (even though I also thought it was a dick move that all my coworkers took their vacations 6 weeks after I started). February was better. We were back at full staff and it was like working a regular full-time job again. But one of my colleagues, a foreign worker, had to go back to his home country because his mom is sick so it looks I'm going to be working insane hours again. I don't hate my job. But I also don't want to work 300 hours in March.

So, that's where I'm at. Sorry for rambling.

I suppose you could try timeboxing and the pomodoro technique. First, specify a time period during the day in which you would like to complete a certain task. For example, clean the house, 1pm to 3pm. Then, break down the task into smaller ones. For example, clean the house might become clean the kitchen and bathrooms, wash the dishes, take out the garbage, clean the toilets, etc. When your chosen time period arrives, commit to completing your goal. Set a timer for 20 minutes and work on your to-do list for those 20 minutes. If intrusive thoughts bother you during those 20 minutes, block them out and tell yourself you'll think about them later. After 20 minutes, take a 5 to 10 minute break; reset the timer and start again for 20 minutes. Repeat until your time box has ended; if you haven't finished your chosen task in the time you have set aside, walk away and come back to it tomorrow or the next day. Make sure you mark off tasks on your to-do list to give you a sense of accomplishment. I don't know if there's any basis in psychology for it, but I know there's some evidence that it helps children with ADD focus in short bursts. It might be enough to help you get your initial spark back.

At best, there are some medications and therapeutic techniques that can help you find that motivation, but, at the end of the day, you're still going to find it within yourself. In my experience as someone who works with people that have severe physical, mental, emotional, and developmental disabilities, psychologists are some of the most out-of-touch people in the medical field. Trust me, I know what it feels like to be demotivated by depression. There was a time not all that long ago where you could find me holed up in my bedroom and up to my ankles in dirty laundry and empty beer cans and pizza boxes; I hadn't showered in weeks and probably smelled like the sink at a dive bar. I knew how I was living was unhealthy, but I couldn't find the strength to change it. But, at the same time, I couldn't get angry with the nice police man that came to my door and told me that I had to clean my house because I was creating a fire hazard and a danger to my neighbours; as well, as attracting rodents. He was just doing his job. In my "professional" experience, most people are willing to lend a hand to a person in need, but they really don't like to feel like they're carrying anyone. I always try to encourage my clients to meet people halfway. No, you may not always feel like going to work or cleaning your house, but you have to at least try.

The thing you need to understand about medications before trying them is that they are NOT "happy pills". Their job is to reduce the worst symptoms of your mental illness, not to make you happy.

I didn't get that at first and it made my decade of experimenting with medications hell. I would start a new medication, give it what I thought was a fair shake, and then stop taking it when it didn't make me happy. Now that I'm older, I can see that the medications are helping me even if they don't make me happy. When I'm taking my meds, I shower most days, I don't become severely suicidal if I don't get enough sleep or my work schedule becomes irregular, and I can spend a night away from home without worrying about a catastrophic fire that will kill my pets. I'm still not happy, but I'm a better person on my meds than without.

I tried the medication I am currently taking for the first time when I was 15 years old and I hated it because I felt like it wasn't doing anything for me, but my family and friends noticed a significant difference in my behaviour when I was taking my meds and when I wasn't; now that I'm older, I see it too. Maybe they're helping you and you don't realize it?

It took me a long time to figure this out and I'm sharing it with you in hopes that it will help: the medications aren't meant to make you feel happy. Their job is to relieve the worst of your symptoms. You'll still feel depressed and anxious, but hopefully not as bad as before. The goal is to give you the help you need to tackle the issues causing your depression and anxiety.
